title: Gold in rags
hookLine: Buddha-nature like gold wrapped in dirty rags, or honey guarded by bees (Tathagatagarbha Sutra)

cards: A lump of baked clay sits on a workshop floor, black from the furnace, cracked, the kind of thing you'd sweep out with the ashes. A smith picks it up and taps it with a hammer. The clay falls away in pieces.

Inside is a statue of the Buddha, cast in gold. The mold was only what the gold was poured into. That picture sits in a short Mahayana sutra, the Tathagatagarbha, beside another: a golden statue wrapped in filthy rags.

teach.b: Back on day eleven hundred two, this path met the teaching itself: every living being carries Buddha-nature, covered but never lost. Today, how the sutra paints it, and what the pictures ask of the one looking.
The rags: a traveler carries a golden statue through rough country and dies on the road. The statue lies in the dirt in rotten cloth. People step over it; nobody passing by sees what it is.
Someone with clear eyes has to see it and have it unwrapped.
The bees: honey hangs in a tree, guarded by a swarm. Someone who wants it doesn't attack the honey. They find a skillful way past the bees.
The house: a poor family lives over buried treasure. The treasure can't speak up and say, I'm here, so they stay poor, standing on gold.

teach.h: A POOR WOMAN CARRYING A KING.
teach.b: The woman: a poor, lonely woman, looked down on by everyone, carries a child who will become a king. She doesn't know it. She thinks of herself the way the street thinks of her.
Lay them side by side and a pattern shows. The covering is real: rags rot, bees sting, poverty hurts.

And the treasure can't announce itself. Someone has to see past the covering, and the sutra says that's what a Buddha does, looking at beings and seeing what they carry. The rags don't make the statue less gold.
They just make it very easy to step over.

how: In East Asian and Tibetan Buddhism, the similes of the Tathagatagarbha Sutra are used in teaching about Buddha-nature, and teachers point to them when encouraging respect for every being.

o: riches someone has kept hidden from others
a holy statue dressed in plain cloth on purpose
Buddha-nature, real but hidden under a covering

games.q: the pictures in the sutra: tap the pairs.
p: wrapped in rotten rags on the road
guarded by a swarm of bees

s: in the sutra, the treasure under the house tells the family it's there
the treasure can't speak. the family stays poor, standing on gold.
in the pictures, the coverings are harmless
rags rot, bees sting, poverty hurts. the covering is real, but it isn't the treasure.
the sutra says a Buddha looks at beings and sees what they carry
like the one with clear eyes who unwraps the statue.

games.q: you're a smith. on the floor is a cracked, blackened lump of clay, fresh from the furnace. what do you do with it?
o: sweep it out with the ashes
break it open with a hammer
polish the outside of the clay
games.why: the smith taps it open, and inside is a golden Buddha. in the sutra the mold is the covering, and the gold was there all along.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose rags are obvious to you, rude, careless, worn out, hard to like, and notice the rags plainly, without pretending they aren't there. Then gently look past them, the way the smith looks at the clay.
You don't need to see the gold clearly; only allow that it might be there.

wordCard.voice: Gold in rags. In the Tathagatagarbha Sutra, a golden Buddha statue wrapped in filthy cloth: a picture of Buddha-nature, covered but never lost. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: gold in the rags. Covered is not the same as lost. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Tathagatagarbha Sutra, the similes (statue in rags, honey and bees, treasure under a poor house, poor woman carrying a future king, gold statue in a clay mold)
